title: Tenant-safe quote API with strict validation
context: Sales moved its Java pricing rules into a Python API. A customer sends quantity as a string, another sends true, and a third changes X-Tenant hoping to receive a competitor discount. Quote totals must remain integer cents and every SKU lookup must use server-verified tenant identity. Build a local route that demonstrates validation, dependency injection and authorization without calling an identity provider.
constraints: Quantity 1..100; SKU maximum 40 characters; no unknown JSON fields.
Two tenants share BOOK but unit prices differ: acme 1250 cents, bravo 1500 cents.
Authentication fixture maps known bearer tokens to identity; untrusted tenant header has no authority.
Self-tests use TestClient; no server or paid API.
requirements: Define strict request model; reject booleans and numeric strings.
Inject verified identity through Depends and scope catalog lookup to tenant.
Use server-owned prices and deterministic integer arithmetic.
Prove negative authentication, validation, unknown SKU and tenant-spoof cases.

questions.prompt: How would you implement this endpoint, and what should validation versus authorization decide?
questions.answer: I would give the endpoint a Pydantic request model containing only SKU and quantity, with extra fields forbidden. Quantity should use a strict integer type because Python treats booleans as integers and loose coercion may accept strings. Bounds belong in the contract. A dependency verifies the credential and returns a tenant principal; the body and X-Tenant header never choose that principal. The route looks up the price by the pair of trusted tenant and SKU, then multiplies integer cents by quantity. An invalid credential returns 401, an invalid request 422, and an unavailable SKU 404. Production authentication would validate issuer, audience, expiration and signature using a maintained identity integration. The fixed-token fixture exercises the boundary and must never be described as production security.
checks: Strict integer rejects true and string 2.
Price lookup includes verified tenant.
Separates 401, 422 and 404 contract failures.

questions.prompt: What would you test before letting Java consumers switch to this Python API?
questions.answer: I would build a contract suite that makes the same requests through the old Java service and new Python route and compares normalized business outputs, including integer rounding rules. The local fixture proves acme receives 2500 cents for two BOOK units even when X-Tenant says bravo. It also proves bravo uses its own price, missing credentials fail, quantity zero and 101 fail, and an injected tenant field fails. A dependency override can isolate the pricing path, but a separate suite must exercise real credential verification. I would include response schema, error shape, correlation identifiers and generated OpenAPI review, then consumer tests for the Java client. Migration rollout would use read-only shadow comparisons before shifting traffic; local TestClient success alone does not establish latency, provider availability or deployed access control.
checks: Includes parity with Java business rules.
Tests override cleanup and real auth separately.
Treats client tests as contract evidence, not deployment proof.

hints: Start with a strict quantity field; type(True) is bool even though isinstance(True,int) is true.
Make verified_tenant one replaceable dependency and never read X-Tenant for authority.
Use a spoofed header and an extra tenant body field as separate negative tests.
acceptance: Acme quantity 2 produces total_cents 2500 despite X-Tenant bravo.
Missing credential returns 401 and unknown SKU 404.
Quantities 0,101,true,"2" each return 422.
Extra tenant field returns 422; dependency override is cleared after testing.
pitfalls: Passing tenant straight from body bypasses authentication.
Using floating-point dollars introduces unnecessary rounding ambiguity.
twist: A contract now allows decimal kilogram quantities. Propose a versioned Decimal quantity contract and explain how you preserve existing integer consumers.
solution: Implement the application factory first so each test has isolated catalog state. Define QuoteInput with a bounded uppercase SKU and StrictInt quantity; forbid extra fields rather than silently ignoring authority-looking input. Define verified_tenant as the authentication seam, using only known fixture credentials in this tutorial. Create the route with Depends, lookup the server-owned catalog by tenant and SKU, and return tenant plus total cents. Run the supplied test client fixture before changing the code. Then remove strictness deliberately and confirm the boolean/string tests expose the regression. Restore strictness, add a third tenant with no price, and require 404 without returning another tenant's price. Finally write the Java migration contract checklist and distinguish fixture authentication from a real verifier. This sequence teaches request shape, policy ownership, framework dependency injection and consumer compatibility together. Framework package installation is needed only to execute the Python file; the scenario, answers and code remain readable offline.

assignment.objective: Build and test a strictly validated, tenant-scoped pricing endpoint.
steps: Save every bundled file into one local exercise directory, including requirements-tested.txt.
Write the request model and application factory from a blank file.
Implement the trusted credential dependency; reject arbitrary tokens.
Add price lookup and integer-cents response.
Add all acceptance fixtures using TestClient.
Change one policy intentionally, observe failing tests, restore it and record what protected the boundary.

title: Retry-safe document job submission
context: A Java client submits document work, times out after the database commit, then retries three times. The current FastAPI route launches three expensive jobs. Product wants a stable job ID across retries, but reuse of the same key for different document text must fail. Job status must survive a web-process restart and remain invisible to other tenants.
constraints: Idempotency namespace is tenant plus key; key maximum 80 characters.
Document fixture maximum 500 characters.
202 means accepted/pending, not completed.
SQLite file lives in TemporaryDirectory; worker only simulates a conditional state transition.
requirements: Persist payload fingerprint and stable job ID atomically before acknowledgment.
Return existing job for equivalent request and 409 for conflicting payload.
Filter status reads by verified tenant.
Demonstrate replay after app recreation and one allowed pending-to-succeeded transition.

questions.prompt: Where should idempotency live, and what does a successful HTTP retry guarantee?
questions.answer: Idempotency must be recorded at the durable business boundary, not only in a process dictionary or a Java client retry flag. I would scope the key by verified tenant and compute a deterministic digest of the validated request. In one transaction, read the key, return the existing ID when the digest matches, reject a changed payload with 409, or create a pending job protected by a unique tenant/key constraint. Commit before acknowledging 202. A retry then guarantees stable submission identity, not exactly-once execution of arbitrary downstream effects. The worker must claim work safely and propagate a stable effect key to external systems. If the external operation times out after taking effect, its reconciliation contract decides whether retry is safe. The fixture demonstrates durable submission and conditional transitions; it does not include a broker or an actual document processor.
checks: Unique key is scoped to verified tenant.
Digest comparison distinguishes equivalent and conflicting retries.
202 and exactly-once external effects are not conflated.

questions.prompt: How would you investigate duplicate jobs that appear only during concurrent requests?
questions.answer: I would collect request IDs, trusted tenant IDs, idempotency keys, payload digests and committed job IDs while excluding document text from ordinary logs. Then I would reproduce two simultaneous submissions against the actual production database engine, with a barrier before insertion, rather than relying on sequential TestClient calls. A read-then-insert without a unique constraint has a race; a constraint alone still requires the losing request to recover by reading the winning row and checking its digest. SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE serializes this teaching fixture, but that locking behavior cannot substitute for PostgreSQL or MySQL evidence. I would also inspect proxy retries, worker claims and downstream effect IDs because stable job submission does not prevent a worker from duplicating effects. Restart tests and injected failure after commit should verify the lost-response path separately from insertion contention.
checks: Uses concurrent database-specific reproduction.
Handles losing unique-constraint contender with digest comparison.
Separates duplicate submissions from duplicate worker effects.

hints: Define identity as (trusted tenant, key), then define equivalence as matching validated-payload digest.
Store pending job and replay metadata in one transaction before returning 202.
Recreate the app against the same temporary database; a process dictionary would fail this test.
acceptance: First and equivalent retry return 202 with the same ID; retry reports replayed true.
Same key with different document returns 409.
Other tenant status lookup returns 404.
App recreation preserves ID; transition executes once; total rows remain one.
pitfalls: Using a global key leaks collisions across tenants.
Calling BackgroundTasks durable delivery loses jobs on crashes.
twist: An external OCR vendor accepts no idempotency key. Design reconciliation states for timeout-after-effect without blindly resubmitting.
solution: Start by writing the table schema and unique tenant/key constraint. Keep the database location supplied to the application factory, allowing a fresh app instance to reuse existing records during the restart fixture. Validate the request, create its canonical JSON fingerprint, and use an explicit transaction to compare or insert. Expose a status route whose predicate includes both ID and trusted tenant. The supplied worker function models a compare-and-change transition, returning the number of changed rows so a second completion attempt is observable. Run the tests and inspect the row count after every replay. Next add a failed state and write the transition table before adding another route; terminal failures should not silently become new work under the same request identity. Document the remaining production requirements: leases, retries, outbox dispatch, backpressure, database contention tests and downstream effect reconciliation. Download both included Python files together because this assignment reuses the tested tenant dependency.

"""Durable local job submission, no broker/provider. Requires FastAPI/Pydantic 2/httpx.
SQLite fixture proves sequential contracts; production concurrency requires its DB tests.
"""
import hashlib
import json
import sqlite3
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Header, HTTPException
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field
from fastapi_tenant_quotes import verified_tenant

class JobInput(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")
    document: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=500)

def create_app(database):
    with sqlite3.connect(database) as db:
        db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS jobs (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, tenant TEXT, key TEXT, digest TEXT, document TEXT, state TEXT, UNIQUE(tenant,key))")
    app = FastAPI()

    @app.post("/jobs", status_code=202)
    def submit(body: JobInput, tenant: Annotated[str, Depends(verified_tenant)],
               key: Annotated[str, Header(alias="Idempotency-Key", min_length=1, max_length=80)]):
        digest = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(body.model_dump(), sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")).encode()).hexdigest()
        with sqlite3.connect(database, timeout=2) as db:
            db.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
            existing = db.execute("SELECT id,digest,state FROM jobs WHERE tenant=? AND key=?", (tenant,key)).fetchone()
            if existing:
                if existing[1] != digest:
                    raise HTTPException(409, "Key reused with different request")
                return {"id": existing[0], "state": existing[2], "replayed": True}
            cursor = db.execute("INSERT INTO jobs(tenant,key,digest,document,state) VALUES(?,?,?,?,?)", (tenant,key,digest,body.document,"pending"))
            return {"id": cursor.lastrowid, "state": "pending", "replayed": False}

    @app.get("/jobs/{job_id}")
    def status(job_id: int, tenant: Annotated[str, Depends(verified_tenant)]):
        with sqlite3.connect(database) as db:
            row = db.execute("SELECT state FROM jobs WHERE id=? AND tenant=?", (job_id,tenant)).fetchone()
        if row is None:
            raise HTTPException(404, "Job not found")
        return {"id": job_id, "state": row[0]}
    return app

def complete_one(database, job_id):
    # Simulated worker: state transition only. Real effects need downstream idempotency.
    with sqlite3.connect(database) as db:
        return db.execute("UPDATE jobs SET state='succeeded' WHERE id=? AND state='pending'", (job_id,)).rowcount

def self_test():
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
        path = str(Path(directory) / "jobs.sqlite3")
        headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer fixture-acme", "Idempotency-Key": "order-7"}
        with TestClient(create_app(path)) as client:
            first = client.post("/jobs", headers=headers, json={"document": "hello"})
            replay = client.post("/jobs", headers=headers, json={"document": "hello"})
            assert first.status_code == replay.status_code == 202
            job_id = first.json()["id"]
            assert replay.json()["id"] == job_id and replay.json()["replayed"]
            assert client.post("/jobs", headers=headers, json={"document": "changed"}).status_code == 409
            assert client.get(f"/jobs/{job_id}", headers={"Authorization": "Bearer fixture-bravo"}).status_code == 404
        # New app instance simulates web-process restart; records survive.
        with TestClient(create_app(path)) as client:
            assert client.post("/jobs", headers=headers, json={"document": "hello"}).json()["id"] == job_id
            assert complete_one(path, job_id) == 1 and complete_one(path, job_id) == 0
            assert client.get(f"/jobs/{job_id}", headers=headers).json()["state"] == "succeeded"
        with sqlite3.connect(path) as db:
            assert db.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM jobs").fetchone()[0] == 1
    print("PASS: replay, conflict, restart, ownership, conditional transition")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    self_test()

title: Lifespan workers with bounded queues and cancellation
context: A document enrichment endpoint creates an untracked asyncio task for every request. During a 300-request burst, memory grows and shutdown leaves half the tasks running. Operations asks for bounded admission, explicit queue-full responses, owned resources and cleanup when cancellation arrives. You must demonstrate the mechanism without downloading a model.
constraints: Two worker tasks; queue capacity two; cooperative simulated work.
429 on full queue with Retry-After 1; queued work is not durable.
Use lifespan to create loop-bound resources and cancel workers at shutdown.
A fixture-only release route controls deterministic queue saturation; never deploy it.
requirements: Create queue, gate and worker tasks within application lifespan.
Reject before adding state when the queue is full.
Maintain active count and task_done in finally, including cancellation.
Prove queue bounds, work completion, closed state and cancellation cleanup.

questions.prompt: How would you replace fire-and-forget tasks with controlled work ownership?
questions.answer: I would choose a durable broker for business-critical jobs, but for short best-effort enrichment I can demonstrate bounded in-process ownership. The application lifespan creates a queue with a finite capacity and a fixed worker set after the event loop exists. Admission uses a nonblocking put and returns 429 with Retry-After when capacity is exhausted, instead of allowing memory to grow without limit. Workers acquire work, increment active accounting, perform cooperative work, and release accounting in finally. Cancellation must propagate after cleanup rather than being swallowed. Shutdown cancels and awaits the owned tasks. Queued and interrupted work must be marked cancelled or otherwise reconciled. The queue exists only in one process, so two web workers mean two independent capacities and a crash loses accepted work. Those limits belong in the API contract and production architecture decision.
checks: Creates loop-bound resources during lifespan.
Finite queue and fixed worker set constrain admission.
Cancellation propagates after finally cleanup.

questions.prompt: Why would async def still produce bad latency, and how would you prove the cause?
questions.answer: An async declaration does not make CPU work or blocking I/O cooperative. A synchronous model invocation, time.sleep, or blocking database driver inside the route can monopolize the event loop. I would measure event-loop lag, queue residence time, active workers, rejection rate and end-to-end percentiles with request IDs. Then compare a slow cooperative fixture against an intentionally blocking fixture under concurrent load. Blocking I/O may be delegated to a bounded thread pool; sustained CPU inference may need separate worker processes or an inference service, with its own queue limits. Cancellation of an awaiting coroutine does not necessarily stop an already-running thread or external request, so releasing an admission permit too early can over-admit physical work. The provided asyncio.sleep fixture verifies cooperative bookkeeping only, not CPU isolation, thread cancellation or production throughput.
checks: Identifies blocking calls inside async routes.
Separates queue time from execution time and loop lag.
Does not claim cancellation stops underlying threads.

hints: An asyncio.Queue(maxsize=2) limits waiting work, not total running work.
Keep queue and tasks in lifespan; TestClient must be used as a context manager.
Put active decrement and queue.task_done inside finally, then re-raise CancelledError.
acceptance: Paused fixture accepts two jobs and rejects third with 429/Retry-After.
Queue status reports exactly two waiting jobs before release.
After release both jobs succeed and active never exceeds two.
Cancellation leaves active zero and queue.join completes; lifespan closed flag is true.
pitfalls: Untracked create_task gives no shutdown ownership.
Treating cancellation of a coroutine as proof a CPU thread stopped.
twist: Accepted jobs now require survival across process crashes. Replace in-process queue with durable admission and explain worker leases.
solution: Implement the lifecycle before the endpoint. An async context manager initializes the bounded queue and an event gate, starts exactly two worker tasks, and keeps their handles. The endpoint reserves queue capacity with put_nowait; it must not create a job record if admission fails. The worker updates its state before the cooperative await, then uses finally to decrement the active count and mark queue completion. A separate cancellation fixture waits until work is active, cancels the worker, and checks both state and accounting. The TestClient fixture holds workers paused so queue-full behavior is deterministic, releases them, polls within a bounded deadline and exits the client context to exercise shutdown. This is an executable lesson in resource ownership and backpressure, not a complete job platform. A production design should remove the test release route, add trusted admission identity and quotas, and choose explicit loss semantics before promising 202 durability.

"""Bounded in-process work fixture; requires FastAPI/httpx. Not durable job delivery."""
import asyncio
import time
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager, suppress
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Request
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

async def worker(state):
    while True:
        await state.gate.wait()
        job_id = await state.queue.get()
        state.active += 1
        state.jobs[job_id] = "running"
        try:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.01)  # Cooperative fixture, not CPU model inference.
            state.jobs[job_id] = "succeeded"
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            state.jobs[job_id] = "cancelled"
            raise
        finally:
            state.active -= 1
            state.queue.task_done()

def create_app(paused=False):
    @asynccontextmanager
    async def lifespan(app):
        state = app.state
        state.queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=2)
        state.gate = asyncio.Event()
        state.jobs, state.active, state.closed = {}, 0, False
        if not paused:
            state.gate.set()
        tasks = [asyncio.create_task(worker(state)) for _ in range(2)]
        try:
            yield
        finally:
            for task in tasks:
                task.cancel()
            for task in tasks:
                with suppress(asyncio.CancelledError):
                    await task
            for job_id, status in state.jobs.items():
                if status == "queued":
                    state.jobs[job_id] = "cancelled"
            state.closed = True
    app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

    @app.post("/jobs", status_code=202)
    async def submit(request: Request):
        state = request.app.state
        job_id = len(state.jobs) + 1
        try:
            state.queue.put_nowait(job_id)
        except asyncio.QueueFull:
            raise HTTPException(429, "Queue full", headers={"Retry-After": "1"})
        state.jobs[job_id] = "queued"
        return {"id": job_id}

    @app.post("/fixture/release")
    async def release(request: Request):
        # Test-only control. Do not expose this route in a deployed service.
        request.app.state.gate.set()
        return {"released": True}

    @app.get("/status")
    async def status(request: Request):
        state = request.app.state
        return {"queued": state.queue.qsize(), "active": state.active, "jobs": state.jobs}
    return app

async def cancellation_test():
    from types import SimpleNamespace
    state = SimpleNamespace(gate=asyncio.Event(), queue=asyncio.Queue(2), active=0, jobs={1:"queued"})
    state.queue.put_nowait(1)
    state.gate.set()
    task = asyncio.create_task(worker(state))
    await asyncio.sleep(0)  # Worker reaches cooperative sleep with active=1.
    assert state.active == 1
    task.cancel()
    with suppress(asyncio.CancelledError):
        await task
    assert state.active == 0 and state.jobs[1] == "cancelled"
    await asyncio.wait_for(state.queue.join(), timeout=1)

def self_test():
    app = create_app(paused=True)
    with TestClient(app) as client:  # Context manager enters and exits lifespan.
        assert client.post("/jobs").status_code == 202
        assert client.post("/jobs").status_code == 202
        overflow = client.post("/jobs")
        assert overflow.status_code == 429 and overflow.headers["retry-after"] == "1"
        assert client.get("/status").json()["queued"] == 2
        client.post("/fixture/release")
        deadline = time.monotonic() + 2
        while time.monotonic() < deadline:
            result = client.get("/status").json()
            assert result["active"] <= 2
            if list(result["jobs"].values()) == ["succeeded", "succeeded"]:
                break
            time.sleep(0.005)
        else:
            raise AssertionError("Fixture jobs did not finish")
    assert app.state.closed and app.state.active == 0
    asyncio.run(cancellation_test())
    print("PASS: bounded queue, rejection, lifecycle, cooperative cancellation")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    self_test()

title: Streaming response holds database connections
context: A support assistant streams tokens for 45 seconds. Its authentication dependency opens a database session with yield and keeps the session until streaming ends. At 100 streams, a 30-connection pool saturates even though each permission check finishes in 8 ms. Older framework versions released dependencies at different times; an upgrade changed resource residence.
constraints: 30 database connections; 100 concurrent streams; permission query 8 ms.
Generator may need document data after endpoint returns.
Permission revocation policy must be explicit for long streams.
No code assignment: reason from lifecycle and draw resource ownership.
requirements: Identify dependency lifetime for the installed FastAPI version.
Separate short identity lookup from stream-owned resources.
Specify cancellation, disconnect and revocation behavior.
Design metrics and regression tests for session residence.

questions.prompt: How do you free connections without making the streaming generator use a closed session?
questions.answer: First inspect the installed FastAPI version and the exact dependency scope because yield cleanup timing changed across releases. I would move authentication and permission lookup into a short resource boundary, materialize a small immutable principal and authorized document identifiers, then close that database session before long streaming begins. The generator must not retain lazy ORM objects that still require the closed session. If streaming truly needs later database reads, it should acquire its own short-lived resources at each operation or use an explicitly stream-owned session with a budget. Current FastAPI supports function-scoped yield dependencies, but changing scope blindly can break a generator that still accesses the session. I would define whether authorization is snapshot-based or periodically rechecked and test disconnect cleanup independently.
checks: Checks installed version and cleanup scope.
Removes lazy session-dependent objects from stream inputs.
Defines permission snapshot versus recheck policy.

questions.prompt: What evidence would show the fix worked rather than merely moving the bottleneck?
questions.answer: I would measure connection checkout duration, pool wait time, active stream count, first-token latency and stream completion percentiles before and after the change. A regression test should hold a stream open, verify the authentication connection has already returned, then cancel the stream and verify generator-owned resources close. Another test should provoke an exception after several tokens and check cleanup; headers already sent cannot be converted into a new normal HTTP error response. Load tests need enough overlapping streams to exceed the original pool capacity and must include downstream model or proxy limits. I would also watch memory growth from materialized documents, since closing sessions by copying entire corpora could trade connection pressure for memory pressure. Local unit tests establish ownership contracts, while load evidence establishes the operational effect.
checks: Uses pool checkout duration and wait time.
Tests disconnect and post-header exception cleanup.
Checks memory and downstream limits after fix.

hints: Draw endpoint-return and stream-completion as separate lifecycle events.
Ask which values are plain data and which trigger lazy database access.
Use function scope only when generator needs no yielded session; otherwise separate resources.

title: Atomic order and durable outbox under crash
context: A Django checkout saves an order, then publishes an event. If publishing fails, operations loses the notification; if retry creates another order, customers receive duplicate shipments. questions.prompt: Why use an outbox when Django already provides on_commit?
questions.answer: on_commit schedules a callback after a successful transaction, but the callback is not part of the committed database state and its failure cannot roll back that commit. A process crash after commit can therefore lose an in-memory publish callback. I would insert the order and an outbox record in the same atomic transaction. A dispatcher polls durable unsent outbox rows; on_commit may wake it sooner but polling supplies recovery. Each event gets a stable identity, and consumers deduplicate because a crash after publish but before marking sent can cause redelivery. The request key is unique within trusted tenant and stores a request digest to distinguish replay from a conflicting new payload. Database constraints enforce uniqueness and positive quantity even when another writer bypasses view validation. """Django 5.2 atomic order + outbox fixture. No message broker or external effect."""
import hashlib
import json
from django.conf import settings
settings.configure(SECRET_KEY="offline-fixture", INSTALLED_APPS=[],
    DATABASES={"default":{"ENGINE":"django.db.backends.sqlite3","NAME":":memory:"}})
import django
django.setup()
from django.db import IntegrityError, connection, models, transaction

class Order(models.Model):
    tenant = models.CharField(max_length=30)
    request_key = models.CharField(max_length=80)
    digest = models.CharField(max_length=64)
    quantity = models.IntegerField()
    class Meta:
        app_label = "offline_outbox"
        constraints = [models.UniqueConstraint(fields=["tenant","request_key"],name="tenant_request_unique"),
                       models.CheckConstraint(condition=models.Q(quantity__gt=0),name="positive_quantity")]

class Outbox(models.Model):
    order = models.OneToOneField(Order,on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    payload = models.TextField()
    sent = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    class Meta:
        app_label = "offline_outbox"

def place_order(trusted_tenant, key, quantity, wakeups, fail_after_write=False):
    # trusted_tenant comes from verified server identity, not a request tenant field.
    if type(quantity) is not int or quantity <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Quantity must be a positive integer")
    digest = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps({"quantity":quantity},sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
    with transaction.atomic():
        existing = Order.objects.filter(tenant=trusted_tenant,request_key=key).first()
        if existing:
            if existing.digest != digest:
                raise ValueError("Idempotency conflict")
            return existing.pk
        order = Order.objects.create(tenant=trusted_tenant,request_key=key,digest=digest,quantity=quantity)
        Outbox.objects.create(order=order,payload=json.dumps({"order_id":order.pk,"quantity":quantity}))
        # Wakeup is advisory. A periodic dispatcher must scan durable unsent rows.
        transaction.on_commit(lambda: wakeups.append(order.pk))
        if fail_after_write:
            raise RuntimeError("Injected crash before commit")
        return order.pk

def dispatch_fixture():
    # Only local status simulation; real consumers deduplicate by event/order ID.
    return Outbox.objects.filter(sent=False).update(sent=True)

def self_test():
    with connection.schema_editor() as schema:
        schema.create_model(Order); schema.create_model(Outbox)
    wakeups = []
    try:
        place_order("acme","rollback",3,wakeups,fail_after_write=True)
    except RuntimeError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError("Injected failure did not raise")
    assert Order.objects.count() == Outbox.objects.count() == 0 and wakeups == []
    order_id = place_order("acme","buy-1",3,wakeups)
    assert wakeups == [order_id] and Outbox.objects.count() == 1
    assert place_order("acme","buy-1",3,wakeups) == order_id
    try:
        place_order("acme","buy-1",4,wakeups)
    except ValueError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError("Conflicting replay accepted")
    for kwargs in [dict(tenant="acme",request_key="buy-1",quantity=3),dict(tenant="acme",request_key="bad",quantity=-1)]:
        try:
            with transaction.atomic():
                Order.objects.create(digest="x",**kwargs)
        except IntegrityError:
            pass
        else:
            raise AssertionError("Database constraint failed")
    assert dispatch_fixture() == 1 and dispatch_fixture() == 0
    assert Order.objects.count() == Outbox.objects.count() == 1
    print("PASS: rollback, commit callback, transaction-committed outbox, unique/check constraints; no restart proof")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    self_test()

I would choose based on relation shape and inspect the actual serialization access path. Here the required page has one customer per ticket, so a tenant-filtered select_related query with stable ordering and a limit is appropriate.     name = models.CharField(max_length=50)
    class Meta:
        app_label = "offline_queries"

class Ticket(models.Model):
    tenant = models.CharField(max_length=30)
    customer = models.ForeignKey(Customer,on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    subject = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    class Meta:
        app_label = "offline_queries"

def serialize(rows):
    return [{"id":row.pk,"subject":row.subject,"customer":row.customer.name} for row in rows]

def bounded_page(trusted_tenant, limit=50):
    if type(limit) is not int or not 1 <= limit <= 50:
        raise ValueError("Limit outside 1..50")
    rows = Ticket.objects.filter(tenant=trusted_tenant,customer__tenant=trusted_tenant).select_related("customer").order_by("pk")[:limit]
    return serialize(rows)

def self_test():
    with connection.schema_editor() as schema:
        schema.create_model(Customer); schema.create_model(Ticket)
    acme = Customer.objects.create(tenant="acme",name="Acme Buyer")
    bravo = Customer.objects.create(tenant="bravo",name="Bravo Buyer")
    Ticket.objects.bulk_create([Ticket(tenant="acme",customer=acme,subject=f"issue-{n}") for n in range(50)])
    Ticket.objects.create(tenant="bravo",customer=bravo,subject="private")
    # Bad relation fixture: tenant field alone must not expose another tenant's customer.
    bad = Ticket.objects.create(tenant="acme",customer=bravo,subject="bad cross-tenant link")
    with CaptureQueriesContext(connection) as queries:
        slow = serialize(Ticket.objects.filter(tenant="acme").exclude(pk=bad.pk).order_by("pk"))
    slow_count = len(queries)
    assert slow_count == 51
    with CaptureQueriesContext(connection) as queries:
        fast = bounded_page("acme")
    assert len(queries) == 1 and slow == fast and len(fast) == 50
    assert all(row["customer"] == "Acme Buyer" for row in fast)
    assert len(bounded_page("bravo")) == 1
    for limit in [0,51,True]:
        try:
            bounded_page("acme",limit)
        except ValueError:
            pass
        else:
            raise AssertionError("Invalid pagination accepted")
    print(f"PASS: query budget {slow_count}->1, payload parity, bounded page, relation isolation")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    self_test()

title: Schema change during zero-downtime rollout
context: A Django service has 12 million orders and four web instances. Product wants status renamed to fulfillment_state with stricter values. A generated migration drops status immediately, but old instances still read it during the rollout and background workers deploy later. A long backfill could lock tables and exceed the maintenance window.
constraints: 12 million rows; old/new web and worker versions overlap.
Rollback possible for seven days after web deployment.
Database engine and lock behavior must be measured, not assumed.
No executable assignment; produce ordered rollout and parity checks.
requirements: Design expand/backfill/contract stages.
Define dual-read/write behavior and source of truth.
Batch backfill with resumable progress and observability.
Keep rollback compatible until old workers retire.

questions.prompt: How would you separate data migration from application rollout?
questions.answer: I would expand the schema first by adding a compatible nullable fulfillment_state column without removing status. New application code would read the new field only when populated and otherwise use an explicit mapping from the old value. During the overlap window, writes must keep both representations consistent through one chosen service boundary or database mechanism; multiple unsynchronized writers are a risk. Backfill runs in bounded batches with resumable progress, rate limits and validation of unmapped legacy values. Then switch reads after parity metrics show coverage and deploy all background workers before making the new field required. Contracting the old column happens only after the rollback window and old-version retirement. Exact DDL lock cost depends on the production database and operation, so I would rehearse against a representative copy and inspect execution plans and lock duration.
checks: Expand precedes code/backfill/contract.
Defines overlapping writer consistency.
Delays destructive contract until rollback window closes.

questions.prompt: What rollback evidence would you require?
questions.answer: I would verify that an old application instance can still deserialize and update rows produced by the new version throughout the seven-day rollback window. Golden fixtures must cover every old status, null new values, unmapped legacy values and conflicting representations. A read-only validation job should compare counts and mapped values by partition rather than claiming success from total row count alone. Rollback routing must consider background workers and newly accepted jobs, not only web traffic. I would test interrupted backfill resume, repeated batches and concurrent updates so a stale batch does not overwrite newer values. Operational evidence includes lock wait, replication lag, error rate and batch progress. A Django migration marked reversible is not sufficient: rollback is safe only if the old code and data contract still work together under the actual overlap plan.
checks: Tests old code against new-version data.
Includes interrupted/resumed backfill and stale updates.
Reversibility flag is not treated as full rollback proof.

hints: A rename can be destructive when old and new binaries overlap.
Keep old field until all readers/writers and rollback window finish.
Backfill needs value parity and conditional updates, not only progress percentage.
acceptance: Plan shows schema expansion before mixed-version deployment.
Fixture matrix includes old-code reads/writes of new-version rows.
Backfill interrupted/resumed twice without overwriting a newer update.
Contract stage gated on parity, old worker retirement and rollback expiry.
pitfalls: Dropping old column before delayed workers upgrade.
Large unbounded backfill holding one long transaction.
twist: Legacy status values cannot map one-to-one. Introduce a quarantine/review path and explain which transactions may proceed.
solution: Write the old-to-new state mapping and identify values that require human or domain review. Create the additive migration, deploy compatibility reads and controlled writes, then start a batch backfill with explicit checkpoints and concurrency-safe predicates. Every batch should record scanned, changed, unmapped and conflicted rows while keeping transaction residence short. Validate parity using samples and partition counts as well as exact mapped-value comparisons. Rehearse old and new web plus worker versions running together, including retries and delayed jobs. Keep old data available for the full rollback window and avoid a contract migration whose timing depends only on web deployment completion. Finally gate the drop on evidence that no active consumer reads the old field and that old-code rollback is intentionally retired. Database-specific DDL rehearsal and lock measurements complete the operational decision; a generated Django migration is only an input to that plan.

title: Lost updates in concurrent balance adjustments
context: Two Django requests read account balance 1000, each subtracts 700, and both save balance 300. One debit disappears, and another code path permits negative balances. The team proposes select_for_update but tests only SQLite, where row-lock behavior differs from production PostgreSQL.
constraints: Balance integer cents; no overdraft allowed.
Two simultaneous debit requests; retry has stable operation ID.
Production PostgreSQL; SQLite fixture cannot establish row-lock semantics.
Debit effect and ledger entry must agree atomically.
requirements: Define atomic conditional debit or locked transaction.
Protect operation identity and balance invariant in database.
Pair balance mutation with ledger entry transactionally.
Propose production-engine concurrency barrier test.

questions.prompt: Would you use F expressions, conditional updates or select_for_update?
questions.answer: An F expression avoids a stale read-modify-save calculation by applying arithmetic in the database, but an unconditional decrement still allows overdraft. For a simple debit I would use an atomic conditional update that filters balance at least the debit amount and inspect the affected-row count. A database check constraint protects the nonnegative invariant against other writers. If the operation needs several dependent reads and writes, a short atomic block with select_for_update may be appropriate on the production engine, with consistent lock ordering and bounded timeouts. The ledger entry and successful debit belong in one transaction, and operation ID uniqueness distinguishes retry from a new debit. I would not infer PostgreSQL row-lock safety from SQLite tests; the chosen isolation level and real contention behavior require engine-specific evidence.
checks: F arithmetic alone does not enforce no-overdraft.
Conditional row count determines success/failure.
Ledger and balance share transaction plus operation identity.

questions.prompt: How would you test the two-request race and retry behavior?
questions.answer: I would run two separate database connections against PostgreSQL, synchronize them with a barrier just before the debit attempt and submit two 700-cent operations against a 1000-cent balance. Exactly one should succeed, one should report insufficient funds, final balance should be 300 and one successful ledger row should exist. A retry of the successful operation ID must return its previous outcome without another debit. Additional tests should cover deadlock or lock timeout classification, a crash before commit and a lost HTTP response after commit. I would verify the constraint with a direct negative update. The application test should not share one ORM connection across threads, and a transaction-wrapped TestCase can hide commit behavior; choose an appropriate transaction test setup. Metrics should expose conflicts and lock waits without logging sensitive account values unnecessarily.
checks: Uses separate connections and synchronized production-engine race.
Tests stable retry ID and ledger agreement.
Includes lost-response-after-commit path.

hints: Lost update comes from reading value before concurrent save.
Atomic arithmetic and overdraft predicate solve different invariants.
Run the race against PostgreSQL with separate connections; SQLite is not row-lock proof.
acceptance: Two 700 debits against 1000 produce one success, one failure, balance300.
Successful operation retry makes no additional debit or ledger row.
Injected precommit failure leaves balance and ledger unchanged.
Direct negative write is rejected by database constraint.
pitfalls: Unconditional F decrement can produce negative balance.
Using SQLite select_for_update tests as PostgreSQL lock evidence.
twist: You must debit two accounts in one transfer. Define lock ordering, transactional ledger representation and idempotent replay.
solution: Describe the balance and ledger invariants before selecting ORM syntax. Choose either an atomic conditional update for the single-account predicate or an explicit lock when the transaction needs broader state, then add nonnegative balance and operation-identity constraints. Keep the ledger write in the same atomic boundary and define the unsuccessful operation response so retries cannot turn into new debits. Build the PostgreSQL concurrency test using separate connections and a barrier, checking final rows after both transactions complete. Add precommit crash, postcommit lost response and repeated operation-ID cases. For transfers, extend the design with stable account lock ordering and paired ledger entries rather than independently debiting and crediting. Finish by documenting isolation level, timeout handling and reconciliation metrics. The answer should demonstrate what each mechanism protects and what remains dependent on the real database rather than treating a locking method name as a complete correctness proof.

title: Cache invalidation leaks stale permissions
context: A Django portal caches document lists under a key containing tenant but not user role or ACL version. After an administrator revokes access, a former reviewer continues receiving cached documents for ten minutes. Another view clears cache before transaction commit, so a concurrent request refills it from uncommitted-old state.
constraints: Revocation target within five seconds; cache TTL ten minutes today.
Tenant, actor scope and permission version affect document visibility.
Commit failures must not publish authoritative new cache state.
Design/debug exercise; no external cache dependency.
requirements: Separate authorization decision from cached data.
Define permission-aware keys and invalidation event timing.
Bound revocation staleness explicitly.
Test rollback and concurrent refill paths.

questions.prompt: How would you redesign the cache boundary?
questions.answer: I would decide authorization on every request using a bounded-fresh permission source rather than treating a cached document list as an access grant. Cached content may be shared where safe, but visibility keys must include the trusted tenant and effective actor or policy scope, plus a version that changes when permissions change. A ten-minute TTL cannot meet a five-second revocation target by itself. Permission changes should commit first, then publish an invalidation/version event; on_commit can trigger an advisory action, while durable outbox handling covers a crash after commit. Cache fills must never make uncommitted permission changes authoritative. I would choose a measurable policy for propagation failures, such as short permission cache TTL or fail-closed checks for protected documents, balancing access correctness against availability with explicit product approval.
checks: Cached content is not authority.
Key includes actor/policy scope and version.
Revocation target exceeds TTL-only capability.

questions.prompt: What failure fixtures would uncover hidden invalidation races?
questions.answer: I would create users with overlapping but different document visibility in the same tenant, warm the cache for each and verify responses cannot cross actor scope. Then revoke one user's access, simulate delayed invalidation and measure when reads stop returning protected documents against the five-second policy. A rollback fixture should change permissions inside a transaction that later fails and confirm no authoritative new version or external invalidation is published. A concurrent refill fixture should pause one request between reading permissions and writing cache while another commits revocation, checking whether the old version can overwrite the new namespace. I would also test dropped events, duplicated events and cache unavailability. Evidence should report maximum observed staleness and fallback behavior, not merely that delete(key) was called once in a unit test.
checks: Tests actor-scope separation within one tenant.
Includes rollback and stale refill after revocation.
Measures staleness, not delete-call count only.

hints: A tenant key distinguishes organizations, not users with different ACLs.
Move invalidation after commit; preserve durable event intent if losing it matters.
Versioned keys prevent a delayed old refill from replacing the current namespace.
acceptance: Two same-tenant users with different ACLs never share protected list output.
Revocation test denies protected access within declared five-second bound.
Rolled-back change emits no new authoritative permission version.
Delayed stale refill cannot overwrite new-version namespace.
pitfalls: Authorizing from cached list membership.
Invalidating before commit and allowing stale concurrent refill.
twist: Cache cluster partition lasts one minute. Choose and justify access behavior for public versus confidential documents.
solution: Map every cached item to the inputs that determine its visibility, including tenant, actor scope, policy version and document version. Separate content retrieval caching from permission decisions so a fast data path cannot become an authorization shortcut. Introduce a commit-generated version or durable invalidation event, and choose a bounded-fresh permission lookup that meets the revocation target even when the content cache is warm. Build the actor-collision and delayed-refill fixtures before tuning TTL. Add transaction rollback and lost-event tests to expose the distinction between callback execution and durable propagation. Measure worst observed revocation delay through the actual read path and document behavior during cache outages or partitions. For confidential data, a failure may require denial rather than returning stale protected content; public data can have a different availability policy. The design is complete only when the product-visible behavior and freshness evidence agree.

title: App factory repairs shared state and error drift
context: A small Flask inventory service initializes global mutable state at import time. Test cases influence each other and malformed JSON returns HTML while the Java client expects JSON. Product needs predictable validation and isolated application configuration before this service becomes a gateway for AI-generated document requests.
constraints: SKU alphanumeric maximum 30; quantity strict integer 0..10,000.
Request body maximum 2048 bytes; exact supported fields only.
Factory creates separate test stores; no external persistence.
Flask 3.1 blueprint and test_client, no server.
requirements: Build create_app factory and inventory blueprint.
Validate content type, JSON shape and strict quantity.
Return stable JSON HTTP error shape and duplicate SKU conflict.
Verify application instances do not share inventory state.

questions.prompt: Why use an application factory instead of an import-time app and dictionary?
questions.answer: An application factory lets tests create independent configuration and state without reloading a module or mutating a shared singleton. I would register the blueprint inside create_app and place fixture inventory in app-owned extensions, accessed through current_app during requests. Importing a blueprint should define routes, not reach into a nonexistent current application. Request validation would require JSON content type, a dictionary with exactly SKU and quantity, a bounded alphanumeric SKU and a strict integer quantity that rejects booleans. An HTTPException handler should preserve the status and relevant headers while returning a predictable JSON shape. In production, app-local memory is not shared across workers and disappears on restart, so inventory would belong in durable storage. The factory improves construction and testing; it does not by itself solve persistence or concurrency.
checks: App-owned state isolates test instances.
Blueprint import avoids current_app access outside request context.
Recognizes process-local store limitations.

questions.prompt: How would you make errors useful to a Java client without exposing internals?
questions.answer: I would document stable machine-readable error codes, HTTP statuses and correlation identifiers, with safe public messages instead of exception traces or database text. Bad media type returns 415, invalid JSON or invalid fields returns 400, duplicate SKU returns 409 and an absent item returns 404. Tests should cover malformed JSON bytes, list instead of object, extra fields, boolean quantity, negative quantity and unknown route errors. The Java consumer should deserialize both success and error shapes and avoid retrying validation failures as transient outages. Internal logs can retain structured exception context under controlled access, while client output remains safe and consistent. The supplied handler derives a response from HTTPException before replacing its body, preserving framework-owned headers such as Allow. I would test method errors and limit errors when expanding the public contract.
checks: Distinguishes 400/415/409/404 behavior.
Keeps internals in controlled logs.
Preserves HTTPException headers and tests consumer parsing.

hints: Move state creation into create_app; importing routes should not create shared test data.
type(quantity) is int rejects bool; exact field set rejects hidden authority-like inputs.
Use error.get_response before changing JSON body so status and headers survive.
acceptance: Create BOOK quantity4 returns201 and GET matches.
Duplicate SKU returns409; malformed JSON and boolean/negative quantities return400.
Plain body returns415; unknown route returns JSON404 shape.
A second app instance cannot see BOOK created in first.
pitfalls: Using module-global mutable store leaks state between tests and processes.
Catching all exceptions and returning200 hides failures from clients.
twist: Inventory now requires durable multi-worker updates. Add a repository interface and transactional conflict contract instead of sharing one Python dictionary.
solution: Create the factory, blueprint and app-owned fixture store first, then implement the POST and GET contracts with narrow validation. Keep error conversion at the application boundary while preserving framework response metadata. Run the supplied test_client cases and inspect the response status as well as body; returning an error-looking JSON object with 200 would still fail the contract. Create a second application instance and prove it has a fresh store, showing why construction ownership matters. Next add a repository seam that the route can use without depending on global variables, and replace the fixture store with a database in a separate extension. Write the Java error parsing examples for malformed requests and duplicate items before discussing retries. This assignment develops API predictability and test isolation. It deliberately leaves durable storage, authentication and multi-worker conflict handling for the follow-up rather than presenting an in-memory inventory as production-ready.

context: A Flask upload route saves a caller filename directly under documents/. A request uses ../../config.txt and another submits a 400 MB file. """Flask 3.1 bounded text upload. Storage only inside self-test TemporaryDirectory.
Extension/UTF-8 checks are not malware detection or document-parser hardening.
"""
import io
import tempfile
import uuid
from pathlib import Path
from flask import Flask, jsonify, request

def create_app(storage):
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.config.update(TESTING=True,MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH=4096)
    storage = Path(storage).resolve()

    @app.post("/documents")
    def upload():
        file = request.files.get("document")
        if file is None or not file.filename:
            return jsonify(error="document required"),400
        if Path(file.filename).suffix.lower() != ".txt":
            return jsonify(error="only txt allowed"),415
        raw = file.stream.read(1025)
        if len(raw) > 1024:
            return jsonify(error="file too large"),413
        if not raw:
            return jsonify(error="empty file"),400
        try:
            text = raw.decode("utf-8",errors="strict")
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            return jsonify(error="UTF-8 required"),415
        if "\x00" in text:
            return jsonify(error="NUL forbidden"),415
        # Client filename is metadata only; generated ID determines storage path.
        document_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
        target = storage / f"{document_id}.txt"
        with target.open("xb") as handle:
            handle.write(raw)
        return jsonify(id=document_id,bytes=len(raw)),201

    @app.errorhandler(413)
    def oversized(error):
        return jsonify(error="request too large"),413
    return app

def self_test():
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
        client = create_app(directory).test_client()
        def send(raw,name):
            return client.post("/documents",data={"document":(io.BytesIO(raw),name)})
        first = send(b"hello","../../escape.txt")
        assert first.status_code == 201
        files = list(Path(directory).iterdir())
        assert len(files) == 1 and files[0].parent.resolve() == Path(directory).resolve()
        assert files[0].name == first.json["id"] + ".txt" and files[0].read_bytes() == b"hello"
        assert send(b"x"*1024,"limit.txt").status_code == 201
        assert send(b"x"*1025,"too-large.txt").status_code == 413
        assert send(b"x"*5000,"request-too-large.txt").status_code == 413
        assert send(b"","empty.txt").status_code == 400
        assert send(b"\xff","bad.txt").status_code == 415
        assert send(b"binary\x00","bad.txt").status_code == 415
        assert send(b"hello","script.py").status_code == 415
        assert client.post("/documents",data={}).status_code == 400
        assert len(list(Path(directory).iterdir())) == 2
    print("PASS: body/file bounds, generated names, UTF-8, empty/rejected uploads")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    self_test()

title: Signed webhook replay and conflicting event IDs
context: A payment-like webhook retries whenever your endpoint times out. Current Flask code hashes reserialized JSON, accepts old signatures indefinitely and records duplicate credits. A provider can send the same event ID again; if payload differs, you need a visible conflict rather than another business effect. Build a local signature and durable replay fixture.
constraints: Tutorial-defined HMAC-SHA256 over timestamp dot raw body.
Freshness window300 seconds; body bound2048 bytes.
Event ID max80; integer amount0..1,000,000 cents.
Trusted fixture secret; temporary SQLite; no real provider or money movement.
requirements: Verify exact raw bytes and strict ASCII hex signature format.
Reject stale, malformed or invalid-signature requests before parsing effects.
Persist event ID and payload digest with transactional replay detection.
Prove replay after app recreation and409 conflict for changed event payload.

questions.prompt: Why verify raw bytes before parsing JSON, and what does signature validation establish?
questions.answer: The provider signs a byte sequence, so parsing and reserializing JSON can change spacing, key order or numeric representation and produce a different signature input. I would read bounded raw bytes, validate timestamp and signature format, then use constant-time comparison against the expected HMAC before parsing supported business fields. A valid signature establishes that someone holding the configured secret authenticated this message under the agreed format; it does not by itself establish freshness, replay safety or permission for every possible event type. Timestamp tolerance handles stale replay within an explicit clock policy, and a durable event-ID record handles duplicate delivery. The tutorial secret and signature format are fixtures, not a real provider integration. Production must follow the provider's exact signing specification, rotation rules, timestamp semantics and event schema, then reconcile accepted events with business state.
checks: Uses raw-body signature, not reserialized JSON.
Separates authenticity, freshness and replay safety.
Rejects malformed/non-ASCII signature before compare_digest.

questions.prompt: How would you avoid duplicate effects when a response is lost after commit?
questions.answer: I would commit an event identity and its exact payload digest before acknowledging success, using a unique event-ID constraint and a transaction that handles concurrent delivery. An equivalent replay returns the recorded outcome without applying the effect again; the same ID with a different digest returns409 and triggers investigation. If applying business state happens in the same database, its update and event record should share one transaction. If an external effect is required, a durable outbox and stable effect identity are needed because receiving the event and performing an external call are not one atomic operation. The fixture stores an amount but moves no money, so its count and sum assertions prove local record deduplication only. I would test process recreation, invalid signature, stale timestamp, malformed JSON, conflicting payload and non-ASCII signature headers to cover lost-response and hostile-input paths.
checks: Commits durable event record before acknowledgment.
Conflict digest differs from valid replay.
External effects need outbox/reconciliation beyond fixture.

hints: Sign timestamp plus raw body; never reconstruct signed JSON.
Validate signature shape before compare_digest to reject malformed Unicode safely.
Use event ID plus digest: same-ID/same-body replay versus same-ID/changed-body409.
acceptance: First valid event reports replayed false; equivalent replay true.
Changed amount under same ID returns409 and row count stays one.
Bad, empty, non-ASCII or stale signatures return401; malformed signed JSON400.
Oversize body413; recreated app returns replayed true; stored sum remains250.
pitfalls: Comparing a non-ASCII attacker signature can raise TypeError without format validation.
Returning200 before durable event recording loses replay identity on crash.
twist: Provider rotates secrets and sends old/new signatures for one hour. Design key selection, bounded overlap and metrics without accepting arbitrary caller keys.
solution: Start with the provider contract and separate byte authentication from business parsing. The reference uses a tutorial-only timestamp-dot-body signing format, an explicit freshness window and strict lowercase ASCII hex shape before constant-time comparison. Parse the authenticated JSON into a narrow event schema and calculate a digest of the raw bytes. Open an explicit SQLite transaction, inspect the existing event identity, return a replay for matching digest, reject conflicting content or insert the first accepted record. A recreated Flask application against the same temporary database proves records survive that app boundary. Run malformed signature, Unicode header, stale timestamp, payload conflict, invalid JSON and body-size fixtures before adding any business effect. Then describe the real deployment requirements: provider-specific signing, secret rotation, clock management, durable transactional business updates and external-effect reconciliation. The supplied code records fixtures only and cannot be mistaken for a payment processor.

"""Flask 3.1 + stdlib signature/replay fixture. No real payment provider.
Signature format is tutorial-defined; use exact provider specification in production.
"""
import hashlib
import hmac
import json
import re
import sqlite3
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from flask import Flask, jsonify, request

FIXTURE_SECRET = b"trusted-offline-fixture-secret-not-production"
FIXTURE_NOW = 2_000_000_000

def signature(timestamp,raw):
    return hmac.new(FIXTURE_SECRET,str(timestamp).encode()+b"."+raw,hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

def create_app(database,now=lambda:FIXTURE_NOW):
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.config.update(TESTING=True,MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH=2048)
    with sqlite3.connect(database) as db:
        db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS events(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,digest TEXT,amount_cents INTEGER)")

    @app.post("/webhooks")
    def webhook():
        raw = request.get_data(cache=True)
        try:
            stamp = int(request.headers.get("X-Timestamp",""))
        except ValueError:
            return jsonify(error="invalid timestamp"),401
        supplied = request.headers.get("X-Signature","")
        if (abs(now()-stamp) > 300 or re.fullmatch(r"[0-9a-f]{64}", supplied) is None
                or not hmac.compare_digest(signature(stamp,raw),supplied)):
            return jsonify(error="invalid signature or stale request"),401
        try:
            body = json.loads(raw)
            if not isinstance(body,dict) or set(body) != {"id","amount_cents"}:
                raise ValueError("Unexpected fields")
            if not isinstance(body["id"],str) or not 1 <= len(body["id"]) <= 80:
                raise ValueError("Invalid ID")
            if type(body["amount_cents"]) is not int or not 0 <= body["amount_cents"] <= 1_000_000:
                raise ValueError("Invalid amount")
        except (ValueError,TypeError,UnicodeDecodeError):
            return jsonify(error="invalid event"),400
        digest = hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()
        with sqlite3.connect(database,timeout=2) as db:
            db.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
            existing = db.execute("SELECT digest FROM events WHERE id=?",(body["id"],)).fetchone()
            if existing:
                if existing[0] != digest:
                    return jsonify(error="event ID payload conflict"),409
                return jsonify(replayed=True),200
            db.execute("INSERT INTO events VALUES(?,?,?)",(body["id"],digest,body["amount_cents"]))
        # Record is durable before acknowledging. No separate side effect in fixture.
        return jsonify(replayed=False),200
    return app

def self_test():
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
        database = str(Path(directory)/"events.sqlite3")
        client = create_app(database).test_client()
        raw = b'{"id":"evt-1","amount_cents":250}'
        def send(client,body,stamp=FIXTURE_NOW,sig=None):
            return client.post("/webhooks",data=body,content_type="application/json",
                headers={"X-Timestamp":str(stamp),"X-Signature":signature(stamp,body) if sig is None else sig})
        assert send(client,raw).json == {"replayed":False}
        assert send(client,raw).json == {"replayed":True}
        assert send(client,b'{"id":"evt-1","amount_cents":251}').status_code == 409
        assert send(client,raw,sig="0"*64).status_code == 401
        assert send(client,raw,sig="é").status_code == 401
        assert send(client,raw,sig="").status_code == 401
        assert send(client,raw,stamp=FIXTURE_NOW-301).status_code == 401
        assert send(client,b"bad json").status_code == 400
        assert send(client,b'{"id":"bad","amount_cents":true}').status_code == 400
        assert send(client,b"x"*3000).status_code == 413
        restarted = create_app(database).test_client()
        assert send(restarted,raw).json == {"replayed":True}
        with sqlite3.connect(database) as db:
            assert db.execute("SELECT count(*),sum(amount_cents) FROM events").fetchone() == (1,250)
    print("PASS: raw-byte signature, freshness, durable replay, conflict and validation")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    self_test()
