title: Session cookies, CSRF and JWT migration confusion
context: A Flask admin portal authenticates with a session cookie. Developers add an API route that updates document permissions and assume JSON content type prevents CSRF. A modernization proposal replaces sessions with a JWT kept in browser storage without explaining XSS exposure or token revocation.
constraints: Permission changes are high-impact; session cookies sent automatically by browser.
Browser UI and server-to-server Java client have different credential transports.
CORS is not authentication or a complete CSRF strategy.
No executable auth fixture; create threat and policy plan.
requirements: Identify credential transport and browser threat separately.
Specify CSRF protection for cookie-authenticated unsafe operations.
Define JWT verifier and revocation assumptions if chosen.
Produce positive/negative browser request fixtures.

questions.prompt: How would you secure the permission update boundary?
questions.answer: I would first identify how the browser supplies credentials. If it automatically attaches an authenticated session cookie, unsafe operations need an explicit CSRF defense appropriate to the application, alongside secure cookie settings and authorization checks. JSON parsing and CORS settings are not substitutes for a complete request-origin policy. The permission route must verify the trusted actor and object scope before mutation. For server-to-server Java callers using an Authorization bearer credential, the CSRF mechanics differ, but token validation and object authorization still apply. Replacing sessions with JWT is not automatically safer: issuer, audience, signature, expiration and algorithm policy require verification, and browser storage introduces XSS consequences. I would use maintained framework integrations and document logout/revocation behavior instead of writing a custom security protocol in a short tutorial.
checks: Distinguishes automatically sent cookies from explicit bearer transport.
Requires authorization in addition to CSRF defense.
Does not treat JWT as automatic security upgrade.

questions.prompt: What tests and evidence would you require before migration?
questions.answer: I would test an authenticated legitimate permission change, missing and invalid CSRF tokens, cross-origin unsafe requests, unauthenticated access and a user changing another tenant's object. Session tests should inspect cookie flags and regeneration behavior at login. JWT tests, if selected, should reject wrong issuer, wrong audience, expiration, invalid signature and disallowed algorithms using the real verifier. Browser integration tests are needed because a backend unit request can ignore browser credential rules. I would include logout and revocation scenarios with stated freshness limits and validate the Java client’s credential path separately. XSS defenses and safe rendering remain necessary regardless of credential format. Migration rollout should preserve authorization semantics and audit evidence; successful token decoding is not proof of permission to mutate an object or of adequate browser protection.
checks: Exercises real verifier and browser credential semantics.
Includes foreign-tenant object and revocation checks.
Separates decoding from authenticated authorization.

hints: Ask whether browser sends credential automatically before choosing CSRF controls.
CORS limits some browser access behavior; it does not verify identity or object permission.
Map session and Java bearer routes separately, then share server-owned authorization policy.
acceptance: Threat matrix names cookie/bearer transports and unsafe operations.
Browser test plan rejects missing/invalid CSRF on authenticated mutations.
JWT plan includes issuer,audience,signature,expiry and algorithm negatives.
Tenant authorization and revocation bounds remain explicit across migration.
pitfalls: Assuming JSON or CORS alone prevents every CSRF path.
Treating decoded JWT claims as verified authority.
twist: An embedded browser client needs cross-site cookies. Revisit SameSite, CSRF tokens, origins and deployment constraints.
solution: Draw the browser and Java caller request paths, including which component stores and sends each credential. Define server-owned authentication verification and object authorization once, then apply transport-specific request protections around it. For the cookie portal, choose a maintained CSRF integration and test unsafe operations with legitimate, missing, invalid and cross-origin requests. For any bearer path, test the real token verifier rather than substituting decoded claims. Add logout/revocation requirements and measure the access freshness they imply. Evaluate browser storage and rendering risk alongside the token format, since JWT storage does not remove XSS concerns. Only after this contract is clear should you choose sessions, bearer tokens or separate routes. The scenario asks for a grounded security plan and evidence matrix, not a custom cryptographic implementation or an assertion that one credential style is universally superior.

title: WSGI worker saturation during long AI calls
context: A Flask gateway has four synchronous workers. Each AI generation occupies one worker for20 seconds; health checks time out when four calls overlap. Team proposes a thread per request and disables timeouts, but model vendor has a hard quota and clients retry lost responses.
constraints: Four workers; generation duration20seconds; burst30 requests.
Accepted business jobs must remain queryable after web restart.
Vendor quota and caller deadline finite.
No provider execution; capacity and queue design exercise.
requirements: Separate web acceptance from durable long-job execution.
Bound queue, workers and vendor calls.
Define idempotent submission and polling contracts.
Provide capacity estimate and health/readiness plan.

questions.prompt: How would you restructure this Flask gateway?
questions.answer: For durable long work I would make the web route validate and authorize the request, persist a job plus dispatch intent, then return202 with a stable status resource. A separate bounded worker pool performs generation under vendor quotas, deadlines and effect-aware retry rules. The API should distinguish queued, running, succeeded, failed and reconciliation-needed states rather than keeping the HTTP connection as its only progress record. Request idempotency prevents retries from creating duplicate jobs. Web health endpoints should not compete with long generation tasks, and readiness should reflect ability to admit work rather than promise every vendor call succeeds. A thread per request merely moves saturation into thread and memory count, while disabling timeouts makes ownership worse. The design needs explicit queue capacity, rejection policy and shutdown/recovery behavior before production deployment.
checks: Durable202 submission replaces long web-worker residence.
Bounded worker/vendor quotas and explicit job states.
Idempotency handles lost-response retries.

questions.prompt: What capacity estimate and test would you present to operations?
questions.answer: With four synchronous workers and twenty-second service time, the idealized ceiling is about0.2 completions per second before overhead, and a burst of thirty jobs cannot meet a short interactive latency target by adding a timeout setting. I would distinguish admission throughput, queue waiting and execution throughput, then measure the real service-time distribution and vendor quota. A load fixture should hold generation calls open, submit thirty requests, and assert health responsiveness, finite queue depth, controlled429 or503 admission responses and stable job identity across retries. Inject a worker crash and restart to verify accepted jobs remain discoverable and reconcile partial effects. Metrics should show queue age, active physical vendor calls, failure/retry amplification and completion percentiles. The estimate is a planning assumption, not a benchmark or guarantee; deployment worker type and infrastructure limits must be measured.
checks: Calculates ideal0.2/s from4/20.
Separates admission, waiting and execution.
Tests health, finite queue and restart recovery.

hints: Four workers busy20seconds cannot serve health quickly through same saturated pool.
202 requires durable accepted identity if restart survival is promised.
Estimate4/20 then include service-time variance, quota and queue age.
acceptance: Plan calculates ideal0.2 completions/s and names assumptions.
Thirty-request fixture keeps health responsive and queue finite.
Retries reuse job ID; overloaded admission returns explicit bounded outcome.
Crash/restart test preserves accepted-job status and effect reconciliation.
pitfalls: One thread per request creates unbounded resource pressure.
Calling an in-memory queue durable202 acceptance.
twist: Product requires interactive first token within500ms. Split streaming reads from durable work and discuss realistic service constraints.
solution: Write an ownership diagram showing web admission, persistent job store, durable dispatch, bounded workers and vendor quota. Define the job state machine and idempotency contract before changing worker counts. Calculate the ideal completion capacity from service time, then model the thirty-job burst with queue waiting and deadline budgets. Build a local fake generation service that can block, fail and report physical active calls; this allows repeatable tests without paid APIs. Keep admission and health behavior measurable while workers are saturated, and reject work when queue capacity or useful deadlines are exhausted. Add restart and lost-response scenarios to prove durable job identity and recovery. Finally compare deployment alternatives using measured throughput and first-token requirements rather than assuming Flask syntax determines all latency. The lesson connects WSGI resource residence, durable job contracts and quota-aware operations in one concrete modernization case.

title: Plugin callback adds SSRF through caller URL
context: A Python modernization plugin accepts a callback URL and posts extracted migration results to it. Customers submit cloud metadata addresses, redirects to internal hosts and very large responses. Team checks that URL begins with https but performs the request before verifying plugin permissions or tenant ownership.
constraints: Plugin results may contain proprietary source summaries.
Only administrator-registered callback destinations allowed.
Network access not performed in this tutorial scenario.
DNS, redirects and egress policies matter beyond string validation.
requirements: Use server-registered destination identities instead of arbitrary URLs.
Authorize plugin action and tenant result ownership before network side effect.
Define redirect,DNS,timeout,size and egress policy.
Design fake transport negative tests and deployment evidence.

questions.prompt: How would you redesign callback destination validation?
questions.answer: I would avoid making arbitrary caller URLs an execution capability. An administrator registers approved destinations, and the request references a server-owned destination ID scoped to the trusted tenant. Before any network call, the service verifies actor permission, result ownership and destination policy. The transport should enforce allowed scheme and host, redirect behavior, bounded timeouts and response sizes, with network egress controls blocking internal and metadata ranges. DNS resolution and redirects can change the effective destination, so a prefix check is inadequate and validation must align with the actual connection path. I would use a maintained HTTP client and carefully reviewed egress integration rather than claiming a short custom URL parser solves SSRF. Proprietary output should be minimized and classified before delivery; a model-generated URL or instruction has no authority to bypass this policy.
checks: Destination ID is registered and tenant-scoped.
Authorization occurs before network effect.
Includes connection-time DNS/redirect and egress boundaries.

questions.prompt: What would your tests prove without contacting internal networks?
questions.answer: I would use a fake transport that records attempted destinations and requires an already-verified policy object. Negative requests with unregistered IDs, foreign-tenant destinations, unauthorized actors or oversized result payloads must fail before any transport call. The transport suite should simulate redirects to blocked hosts, DNS answers in denied ranges, slow responses and oversized bodies, checking bounded termination and no confidential payload delivery. Real deployment evidence must separately verify network egress policy and the HTTP client's resolution/redirect behavior; a fake transport cannot prove those environmental controls. I would record destination ID, policy version, outcome and correlation ID without logging proprietary source content. Retries need stable delivery identity and effect semantics so a lost response does not blindly duplicate a callback. The acceptance claim should state precisely whether policy validation, fake transport behavior or deployed egress was tested.
checks: Negative authorization cases make zero transport calls.
Simulates redirect,DNS,deadline and size failures.
Separates fake transport from deployed egress proof.

hints: A URL is a potential network capability, not harmless metadata.
Use registered destination ID; verify actor, tenant result and destination before calling transport.
Fake transport proves ordering; deployed egress evidence proves network boundary.
acceptance: Unregistered/foreign/unauthorized destination produces zero fake transport calls.
Redirect-to-blocked-host and denied DNS fixture rejected.
Slow and oversized responses terminate within declared bounds.
Evidence labels fake-policy versus deployed-network checks and minimizes output payload.
pitfalls: https prefix does not prevent requests to internal addresses.
Following redirects after validating only original URL.
twist: Customers require self-service destination registration. Design verification and approval workflow that cannot authorize arbitrary internal egress.
solution: Define who may register destinations and what output classes may leave the tenant boundary. Store an approved destination identity and policy version server-side, then make the callback request reference that identity rather than an arbitrary URL. Resolve actor permission and result ownership before any transport operation. Build a fake transport with a recorded-call list so negative policy requests can prove zero attempted effects. Add simulated redirect, DNS, timeout and response-size cases at the transport boundary, while documenting which checks require the real deployment network. Include stable delivery identity and reconciliation behavior for retries, because an HTTP timeout may happen after the receiver processed the callback. Finish with egress configuration evidence, audit metadata and payload minimization. The exercise teaches authority ordering and bounded network effects without contacting internal services or promising that a small URL sanitizer is a complete SSRF defense.
